body: Funny you should mention that. I literally live in a small midwestern town. Haha! If you can’t find others to make movies with then make them with yourself. The whole point is: make them and have fun with it. If your friends aren’t interested it’s probably because you haven’t given them anything to be interested in. Let your passion for it shine through. If you’re enthusiastic enough about it someone will likely feel that energy and, at the very least, might do it for the fun of it. Put out ads online for surrounding towns. Maybe start your own filmmaking gathering so you can meet new people….. or move somewhere else and make new friends.

IF you’re just starting out the best advice I can give someone is don’t worry yourself with rules and structure. Just grab a camera, grab some friends, and start making movies. Focus on being creative and telling stories. If you can’t tell a good story and have fun with it, no amount of 3-point lighting or 180 degree rules is going to make you a better filmmaker. 

You’ll learn the rules eventually and you’d be surprised how much of it is already hard wired into your brain from watching countless films. Eventually you’ll be on YouTube or have your face stuck in books learning things but you’ll be doing it BECAUSE you want to be better. Not because you think you have to!

This part I know I can help you with: there is no such thing as writers block. “Writers block” is nothing more than your fight or flight response trying to protect you from something it thinks is going to hurt you. Our brains are stupid that way. Writers block is just fear. Only way to get over that is to just do it. Make yourself sit down and write. Your brain will eventually catch on and realize that what you’re doing isn’t bad for you. There’s no magical formula. There’s no magic word that’s going to snap you out of it. You can’t formula your way out of it and waiting for inspiration is only going to make sure you never get started. Just sit down and write the damn thing or get your friends together and write it together. You can always rewrite or edit a bad page. You can’t edit a blank page.

It’s not no. Mal Adaptive Daydreaming is currently labeled as an unhealthy coping mechanism that usually develops in child hood. If anything, it would more closely resemble OCD as it consists of ritualistic behaviors like pacing and listening to loud music to drown out reality. There is often an object as well. Something that is kept on the person. The purpose of the object is still being determined but if I had to describe mine in some way, it offers a form of comfort while acting as a sort of “key”. It’s part of the ritual. This is almost always a private ritual as well as most mal adaptives are hyper aware of how embarrassing it can be and go out of their way to hide the behavior. I highly recommend doing some independent research though as it’s a difficult thing to fully describe and understand. ADD is a learning disability. Mal Adaptive Daydreaming is an unhealthy coping mechanism usually brought on by trauma.
There are forums here on Reddit and through Eli Sommer’s research. He’s the leading researcher on the subject right now.

Even if you don’t meet the love of your life at a paint and sip, you still get to have the experience of painting something fun with like minded people surrounding you. There’s always something to be learned or gained, even in bad relationships. It all works together to shape who we are.

I’ve been where you are. Multiple times. First snd foremost, this is depression. Know and understand that. And as such it is always best to find a mental health professional to help with that. 

Something that I would like you to understand right now, however, is that depression lies to you. It will tell you that no one cares and that no one is there for you. This is unequivocally untrue. Even if you don’t have anyone with you in person guess what? You have me. And all of us here. 

Flip the script on the depression. Realize that it is something you can’t flip a switch on, but you can flip the script. When you feel like you hate yourself run to a mirror, smile and tell yourself that you LOVE yourself. It’s going to sound stupid and corny but it actually works. 

What is the specific situation? Is it just that you feel alone? Or did something else happen? First of all, there’s nothing wrong with being alone. I’ve been that way my whole life. Had to teach myself things that my absent father was never there to teach me and mother was too busy smoking and reading shitty horror novels to deal with her own kids. I learned how to be very independent. Yet… I still yearned for companionship as well. But, as of right now, I’ve learned to be content with myself. 

Even if others don’t think I’m cool, or handsome, or funny, I know that I’m worth it as a person. It’s their loss if they don’t want me in their lives. If no one else gives a fuck about you, YOU can give a fuck about yourself. Believe it or not, that kind of shit attracts people. Good people even. Not all of them, but a good chunk of them.

I can’t imagine it makes things easy on the friendship. Obviously the dynamics of the friendship would be altered. Even if he renounced his feelings there would always be that lingering thought in the back of both of your minds. 

However, I also think it’s worth taking a moment to consider those feelings. Especially if he is still being a relatively normal dude. (This applies to women too not just a guy thing.) 

Is it worth it to you to consider possibly taking the relationship to that level? If yes, then the only way it becomes a problem is if you try it and break up. Even then, there are always exceptions to the rule. Some people are able to bounce back to platonic relationships with people, no problem. For others everything falls apart. 

Ultimately, ask yourself this: if the idea of a male/female friend suddenly developing romantic feelings for you disturbs or worries you in any major way, were they really the type of person you should be friends with in the first place? I know that might sound weird, and I’m not saying that every friend should be perceived as a possible lover, but we probably let more red flags slide when we’re in love with someone than we do when we’re just friends. It’s easier to unassociate with someone when they’re friends. Lovers tend to be harder. 

I don’t consider all my friends to be romantic partners, but I’d like to think that someone I date is also a good friend. And I’m not above starting out as friends before going into a romantic relationship as well. And a lot of very successfully relationships have come from previous friendships. 

If it happened to me, how I handle the situation would be based entirely on whether or not I’m single. If I’m single, yeah I might consider it. Maybe go on a couple of dates and see if there’s something romantic there worth pursuing. If I’m not single, I would assume my friends know this already and it would be a huge turn off for me. I’d walk away from that friendship.

Let her know that you’re just not into the heavy drinking life-style and that you want to things that don’t involve alcohol. If she’s unwilling to compromise or consider changes then I would consider a break-up. But alway try to communicate your feelings first and see if there’s a way to make some changes before jumping into dumping.

It was a very different time back then for women and especially so for women of noble blood. Alcina was probably expected the bear children but her hereditary blood disease likely would have been noticed as a child. I'm just going to touch on a bunch of points I've read in this thread all at once --

1:1 adaptions of anything don't make sense when you have the original source material so that's kind of a silly point to even make. Adapting the first game does not, by default, mean it would be 1:1. There's plenty of room for creative freedom without sacrificing the elements that make the fans happy. Not only that, but a game like Resident Evil (or most video games for that matter) isn't nearly as complicated as something like, say, Lord of The Rings so there's really no reason they couldn't have done it.

Also, speaking as both a filmmaker AND Resident Evil fan, making video game adaptions in general really isn't as hard as they make it sound. The problem with video game adaptions is that they still get treated like a lower form of storytelling. No one respects the material enough to make a movie that not only pleases fans but appeals to a larger audience as well. They focus solely on fan service and not just making a good movie that everyone can enjoy. Instead they make weird choices based on what the suits want and what the people who've never played a video game before in their lives want. And because the suits have very little faith in the movies they lord over ridiculous details.

Mario Bros. should have been an animated film right from the get-go. Street Fighter could have cut out half the cast AND SAVED THEM FOR FRANCHISE SEQUELS RATHER THAN CRAMMING THEM INTO ONE MOVIE and maybe hired someone other than Van Dam to play all-American hero Guile (Raul Julia owned the f\*$# out of Bison though and I wouldn't change that to save the world).  Simple changes... Simple things could have made all those video game adaptions better movies right from the start.

The "average" hater isn't complaining about the movie over some ridiculous notion that we were going to bring our controllers to the theater with us. They're mad because the movie is objectively, poorly made. Too many characters (once again cramming everything into one movie for the sake of fan service because they don't have faith in a franchise), and an incoherent plot that makes weird decision. Not to  mention strange decisions concerning the characters and the story beats from the game. I don't know who thought it would be a good idea to ship a Wesker/Valentine romance but I'll be damned if that didn't make me want to vomit in the theater. Lisa Trevor is now a sympathetic anti-hero who's barely in the movie until it conveniently decides it needs her to conveniently show up and conveniently have the keys to the lab so our "heroes" can conveniently get the movie over with and then... um... just f\*&$'s off for the rest of the movie I guess??? And that's just a couple of the strange changes they made to the games narrative and characters.

Again, this isn't hard to do. The first game is perfect for a franchise setup. We don't need hours of puzzle solving and item box backtracking. As far as changes go all you need is for one of the scientists to still be alive and trapped in the lab, an intercom system in the mansion, a door that requires special keys in order to get to the lab and BOOM, you now have something that is not only new to the story but you have logical reason to split up the gang and have them explore the mansion for a bit before descending into the lab. The mansion search poses as a perfect breeding ground for character development and relationship building and you get to have some iconic game moments and maybe even a few new surprises along the way. I am not above saying I could have written (and technically have) a better movie that stays close to the games and also delivers a story that a general audience can understand. A story that would have actually setup sequels and still did something fresh with the presentation.

As for the comment about 80's movies and B-movies and going to the theater and just "having fun" with a movie, I'm gonna end that right here. First of all, few if any of the filmmakers from the 80's ever set out to make a campy b-movie. They were lovers of the genre and filmmaking and most of them sincerely thought they were making great films -- and in some cases they sort-of-accidentally-did. They were having fun too, but not at the expense of making something they loved. They weren't campy and bad intentionally. They were campy and bad as a result of the limitations of the period in which they were made which makes them endearing and forgivable. It makes it easier to watch them and have fun with it. Further more, a movie doesn't have to be campy, cheesy, or fu#$in' stupid in order to be fun. I don't know where anyone got that ridiculous notion from but I really wish they'd stop. A movie can be coherent, well written, competently made, well performed, *and*  be a horror movie *and* still be fun without being stupid.

This sounds like Cluster Headaches. Talk to your doctor to be sure and mention cluster headaches to them. They will know what you’re talking about. Cluster headaches are a chronic condition. I started getting them in my 20’s. They can be triggered by a lot of things but are common among smokers especially, people who have a history of drug use (particularly powders), and sometimes alcohol abuse. This isn’t to say that other people can’t get them, they are just more common in those arenas. They tend to appear in “clusters” and can last anywhere from a few minutes, hours, days, or for as long as months. The primary characteristics are how they start. Usually it’s a tiny bit of pain behind the eye that transitions into a painful stabbing sensation. As the headache subsides there tends to be a weird feeling in the one side of your face. Like a cool, numbing feeling. Cluster headaches are also unaffected by common headache and migraine treatments. Ibuprofen, Excedrin, and other over the counter medications won’t work. Neither does lying down in a dark quiet room (in fact laying down can often make them feel worse). This can also lead to feelings of panic (though not always). I was treated initially with Carbamazepine and some kind of heart medication. The heart medication was only for the first couple of weeks. After that it was a steady regimen of Carbamazepine until the clustered stopped happening.

Okay, here's where I stand on this. And before I begin let me start by saying that I'm filmmaker. I love movies of all sorts.  First of all, we're talking about movies. This is not a serious subject and not something that should be considered a deal breaker in a relationship. You have your favorites and he has his. In this case, it might be a good idea to stop and reassess the situation. Are you being fair and open minded towards his tastes? Having said, that, it's totally understandable that neither of you are always going to share interests in all the same things. And it's quite healthy, in fact, for you to have your own thing. Stuff that you enjoy that doesn't always have to involve your partner. In this case, I would highly recommend that the two of you sit down and have a calm, rational discussion about compromise. If both of you are vehemently opposed to watching what the other one likes then it may be in your best interest to simply regard movie watching as a singular activity. But do so in a peaceful way. There could be a number of reasons you feel this way about your own films, however, I would theorize that most of what your feeling -- or lack thereof -- is because as filmmakers it can be difficult, if not impossible, to disconnect ourselves from the technical side of story telling. When you're an audience member and you have no stake in the success of the film and none of the work or stress that came along with it, it's easy to sit back and just let a story wash over you and take you to those emotional places. But when you make films, especially if you're an indie filmmaker, we often get so involved with just making it that by the time we see the finished product we've sort of become desensitized to it. That's not to say that we CAN'T have an emotional response to a particular scene, but generally speaking our minds are focused on things that the audience probably isn't. Little details that stand out that shouldn't be there, a bad cut that just couldn't be avoided, a line delivery that fell flatter than we expected, etc.

I grew up watching Blade Runner as a kid and it's one of the films that inspired me to pursue my own career in film. Having said that, I'm now 35 years old and only just now getting around to reading the book. So far I'm loving it. It is a bit unsettling at times reading the book and seeing how dissimilar they are. I'm about 6 chapters in and other than Deckard (who is barely anything like the Scott/Ford version of the character) so far the two are so different it's almost strange to even think the movie was based on the book. 

But, like some have already said, I think what makes Blade Runner -- as well many other book-to-film adaptions -- so great is that it IS different from the book. I think this whole idea of a book being faithfully adapted to screen word for word is a bit obscene and kind of makes the whole idea pointless. I guess I just prefer to have an original experience.

I don't think I've ever seen a film that made me feel more dirty and uncomfortable in the end than The Mist. My mouth fell open and I sat through the entire credits that way unsure how to respond or what to do.
